newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European Commission says bans Clabecq aid.
newsitem.headline: European Commission says bans Clabecq aid.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday a rescue plan for Belgian steel firm Forges de Clabecq was unacceptable under European rules for aid to the steel industry.
"The European Commission has declared that the measures taken by the Walloon region in favour of Forges de Clabecq...are incompatible with the common market," it said in a statement.

The measures referred to were Wallonia's offer of 1.5 billion Belgian francs of capital, the granting of 700 million francs of credit, writing off debts of more than 800 million francs and the rescheduling of other debts.
The Commission said the measures were incompatible with EU rules on steel aid which only allowed aid for environmental reasons, for research and development or for closure.
It added that the aid already received by Clabecq must be paid back within two months.
Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told a news conference however the European Union would help revitalise the Walloon region.
"I'd...like to point out that the European Commission will use the means available to it to help the region to do the necessary reconversion," he said.

"Although the decision (to disallow the Clabecq rescue plan) might be called a negative one, there is a positive signal going out that the maximum will be done to help the region to attract other investment which is more likely to bear fruit," he added.

Van Miert noted that when the Clabecq rescue operation was launched the company had almost gone bankrupt, and a report commissioned by the Walloon region said the company was highly unlikely to survive.

The report, by Jean Gandois - chairman of Wallonia's biggest steel maker Cockerill Sambre - showed the poor competitive position of loss-making Clabecq whose costs were 20 to 30 percent above the average of its competitors.

Belgian authorities, which so far have denied the Clabecq rescue plan involved state subsidies, might now apply to the European Commission for clearance of aid. But this would involve the approval of European Union industry ministers as well as of the Commission.
